How Cleaning Products Work, Your Raw Materials and Staying Safe

Before you mix anything, you need to understand what makes a detergent clean, what each chemical in the market does, and how to protect yourself and your family. This module covers surfactants, the common raw materials used in Nigerian liquid soap, and the safety rules for sulphonic acid, caustic soda and bleach.
How detergents clean and which products to start with

Every cleaning product on a supermarket shelf, from dishwashing liquid to laundry detergent, depends on one kind of ingredient: a **surfactant**. The word is short for "surface active agent". A surfactant is a molecule with two very different ends. One end, the **head**, loves water. The other end, the **tail**, loves oil and grease and hates water.
Soap bubbles floating
Foam and bubbles come from surfactants, the working ingredient in every detergent you will make.

When you wash a greasy pot, the oil-loving tails push into the grease. Thousands of surfactant molecules surround each small drop of oil, with their water-loving heads facing outward. Now the grease is wrapped in a coat that water can hold, so rinsing carries it away. This is why plain water cannot remove palm oil from a plate, but water with detergent can.
Soap and detergent are not the same thing

**True soap** is made by reacting fats or oils with a strong alkali such as caustic soda. Bar soap and traditional black soap are true soaps. **Synthetic detergents** are surfactants made in factories, mostly from petroleum or plant raw materials. In Nigeria, the keg "liquid soap" sold for dishes and general cleaning is almost always a synthetic detergent, made from chemicals such as **sulphonic acid** (linear alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, also called LABSA) and **SLES** (sodium laureth sulphate, often sold as "texapon").

Detergents have one big advantage over soap: they keep working in **hard water**. Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium. These react with soap to form the grey scum you see in some bathrooms, and the soap stops foaming. Synthetic detergents are much less affected, which is one reason they took over laundry and dishwashing.

The cleaning agents (surfactants)

**Sulphonic acid** (linear alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, LABSA) is a thick, dark brown, oily liquid. It is the raw form of one of the most widely used detergent surfactants in the world, linear alkylbenzene sulphonate (LAS). It replaced older branched versions because it breaks down more readily in the environment. As bought, it is a **strong, corrosive acid**. It cannot be used on hands or dishes until it is **neutralised** with an alkali, which turns it into its sodium salt, the actual cleaning agent.

**SLES** (sodium laureth sulphate) is usually sold as a thick white or clear paste, often labelled 70%. That number is the **active matter**: 100 g of 70% paste contains about 70 g of actual surfactant and 30 g of water. SLES foams well and is gentler on skin than neutralised sulphonic acid, so it is used in hand wash and added to multipurpose soap. It dissolves slowly; break it up and stir patiently, or soak it in some of the batch water first.

**SLS** (sodium lauryl sulphate) is a related surfactant, usually a powder or needles. It is a strong foamer but harsher on skin than SLES, and its dust irritates the nose and eyes, so wear a dust mask when handling it.

**Foam booster** is a trade name, not one chemical. Ask the seller exactly what it is and request a data sheet. Foam makes buyers happy, but more foam does not mean better cleaning. A product can foam hugely and still leave grease behind.
Colour, perfume and preservative

Use colours and perfumes sold for detergents or cosmetics, not food colour or random oils, because they must stay stable in the product. Add perfume near the end, when the batch has cooled, so the scent is not lost.

A water-based product with thickeners can grow mould and bacteria, especially in a warm climate. That is why it needs a **preservative**. Many local recipes use **formalin**, which is a solution of formaldehyde in water. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies formaldehyde as a human carcinogen. Its vapour also irritates the eyes and lungs. Avoid it. Ask your supplier for a preservative made for detergents or cosmetics, ask for its data sheet and the recommended dose, and follow that dose.
Buy with labels, not just names

Only buy chemicals in containers with a clear label showing the chemical name and, where possible, the strength. Ask for the safety data sheet (SDS). If a seller cannot tell you what is in "foam booster" or "special thickener", do not put it in a product people use on their hands and plates.

Chemical safety: PPE, workspace, bleach rules and first aid
Set up a safe mixing area with the right protective equipment

Sulphonic acid and caustic soda are both **corrosive**: they can burn skin and cause permanent eye damage within seconds. Bleach can release dangerous gas when mixed with the wrong product. None of this means you should be afraid. It means you work with a routine, every single time, so that a mistake is unlikely and a splash is harmless.
A pair of safety goggles
Splash goggles are the most important item you will buy for this business.
Personal protective equipment (PPE)
**Chemical splash goggles** that seal around the eyes. Ordinary glasses leave gaps at the sides.
**Rubber or nitrile gloves**, long enough to cover the wrists. Replace them if torn.
**Long sleeves, long trousers or wrapper, an apron, and closed shoes.** No slippers.
**A dust mask** when weighing powders such as caustic soda, soda ash, STPP or SLS.
Tie back long hair and remove loose jewellery.
Your workspace
Mix outdoors under a shade or in a room with open windows and moving air, never in the kitchen where you cook.
Keep children and animals away while chemicals are out. A locked area is best.
Use plastic drums and buckets (HDPE or PP) or stainless steel. Never use **aluminium**: caustic soda attacks it and gives off hydrogen gas, which can catch fire.
Keep a large container of clean water within reach for rinsing splashes.
Never store chemicals or finished products in drink bottles. Children have been poisoned this way.
Safe mixing order
Caustic soda: measure cold water first, then add the caustic soda slowly to the water while stirring. Never pour water onto caustic soda: it can boil up and splash.
The caustic solution gets very hot. Let it cool before adding it to anything else.
Sulphonic acid: pour it slowly into the water or batch, never the other way round, stirring as you go.
Neutralising acid with alkali gives off heat. Add the alkali in small portions and stir between additions.
Soda ash fizzes when it meets acid (it releases carbon dioxide). Add it slowly so the batch does not foam over.
Bleach: the rule with no exceptions

Household bleach contains **sodium hypochlorite**. Mixed with **acids** (such as many toilet cleaners, vinegar, or sulphonic acid), it releases **chlorine gas**. Mixed with **ammonia** (found in some glass cleaners and in urine), it releases **chloramine gases**. Both cause coughing, chest pain, breathing difficulty and watery eyes, and higher exposures can damage the lungs and kill. The US CDC advises never mixing household bleach with any other cleaners or disinfectants.
Never add bleach to your liquid soap batch or to any product you make.
Never put bleach into a container that once held sulphonic acid or an acidic toilet cleaner.
Tell customers clearly: use bleach on its own, rinse the surface, then use other cleaners.

First aid
What happened
What to do
Splash in the eye
Rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open. Go to a hospital straight after.
Splash on skin
Remove contaminated clothing. Rinse with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Seek medical care if the skin is red, painful or broken.
Breathed fumes or gas (for example bleach mixed with acid)
Leave the area at once into fresh air. Get medical help if coughing, chest pain or breathing difficulty continues.
Swallowed
Do not make the person vomit. Rinse the mouth with water and go to a hospital immediately, taking the container.
No vinegar on burns
Do not try to neutralise a caustic burn with vinegar or an acid burn with soda. The reaction gives off heat and wastes time. Plenty of running water is the correct first aid for both.

**Spills.** If you spill caustic soda solution or sulphonic acid, keep people away, put on your PPE, and soak up the liquid with sand, sawdust or old cloths. Scoop it into a labelled plastic container. Then wash the area with plenty of water. Do not try to neutralise a large spill by pouring the other chemical on it, because the reaction gives off heat and can splash. Never wash concentrated chemicals into a well, borehole area or open gutter.

The stages explained

**Prepare the thickener.** Sprinkle nitrosol (HEC) slowly onto the measured water while stirring, so each grain gets wet separately. If you dump it in, it forms lumps that never dissolve. Many makers leave it to swell for several hours or overnight until the water is clear and thick.

**Dissolve the alkalis separately.** In a separate plastic container, add caustic soda slowly to cold water and let it cool. Dissolve soda ash in water in another container. Keep STPP dissolved separately as well if your formula uses it.
**Add the sulphonic acid.** Pour the sulphonic acid slowly into the thickened water, stirring steadily in one direction. The mix will turn darker and may smell sharp; keep your face back.

**Neutralise slowly.** Add the caustic solution and soda ash solution in small portions, stirring well after each. Soda ash will fizz. The batch will warm up. After each portion, dip a pH strip into a small sample and compare the colour.
**Stop at the right pH.** Aim for close to neutral, around pH 7. Below about 6 means acid remains and the soap will sting hands. Well above 9 means too much alkali, which is harsh on skin.
**Add SLES and builders.** Stir in the SLES (pre-soaked in some batch water helps) and any STPP solution until smooth.

**Adjust thickness, then finish.** If needed, add salt dissolved in water a little at a time (see the next lesson for why). When the batch has cooled, add colour, perfume and preservative at the doses given on their data sheets.
**Rest.** Cover and leave the batch for 12 to 24 hours so foam settles and air bubbles rise. Check pH again, then bottle.
Why pH is measured, not guessed

Sulphonic acid strength and caustic soda purity vary between suppliers and even between drums. A fixed amount of caustic that was right for one drum can leave another batch acidic or too alkaline. Always neutralise in portions and check with pH strips. This is the single most important quality step.
Worked example: correcting the pH during neutralisation
For example, Ngozi in Enugu is making a 20-litre batch using a formula from her trainer. Her sulphonic acid is from a new supplier.
After adding the caustic and soda ash amounts on her sheet, she tests a sample: the strip shows about pH 5.
She knows this means acid is still present, so she does not continue to the SLES stage.
She dissolves a little extra soda ash in water and adds it in two small portions, stirring and testing after each.
After the second portion the strip shows about pH 7. She records the extra amount and the supplier's name in her batch record.
The batch is neutral and safe on hands. Ngozi now knows the new supplier's acid needs a little more alkali, and she will check this again with her next drum.
Bottling

Use clean bottles or kegs with tight caps. Rinse them with clean water and let them drain dry. Never reuse containers that held chemicals, food oil or drinks. Fill to the same level every time, cap tightly, and write the **batch number** on each container or on the label before it leaves your workspace.
Clean as you go

Wash the drum, paddle and jugs with plenty of water as soon as a batch is bottled, while wearing gloves. Dried product and acid residue can contaminate the next batch, and a dirty drum can introduce mould. Keep one paddle and one set of jugs only for soap making, never for food.

Expect your first few batches to look slightly different from a factory product. Colour can vary with the shade of the sulphonic acid, and the batch may look cloudy while foam is still settling. What matters is that the pH is right, the thickness is what you planned, and it cleans well. Those three things are what buyers notice after the first purchase.

Scaling: the one-litre method

Write every ingredient in your formula **per one litre** of finished product. Then any batch size is a single multiplication. To get the per-litre amount, divide each quantity by the batch size the formula was written for.
Worked example: scaling a formula sheet

For example, Halima's trainer gave her a tested 20-litre formula. One line says 100 ml of perfume. She wants a 2-litre test batch first, then a 25-litre production batch. (These numbers are only to show the arithmetic, not a recipe to copy.)
Per litre: 100 ml divided by 20 L = 5 ml of perfume per litre.
Test batch: 5 ml x 2 L = 10 ml of perfume.
Production batch: 5 ml x 25 L = 125 ml of perfume.
She does the same division and multiplication for every line, writes the results in a table, and double-checks each with her phone calculator.
Halima has one table with three columns (per litre, 2 L, 25 L). Every batch size uses the same proportions, so the test batch truly predicts the big batch.
Active matter: how strong is your product?

Two products can look identical but contain very different amounts of cleaning agent. To compare, work out the **active surfactant** in each batch. Multiply the weight of each surfactant raw material by its strength. For example, 1,500 g of 70% SLES paste gives 1,500 x 0.70 = 1,050 g of active SLES. Dividing the total active weight by the batch weight gives the active percentage, which you can use to keep every batch the same and to compare formulas honestly.
The salt curve

Salt thickens products that contain SLES, but only up to a point. As you add salt, the liquid gets thicker and thicker, reaches a peak, and then **gets thinner again** if you keep adding. Makers call this the salt curve. Once you pass the peak you cannot take the salt out; you can only add more of the other ingredients to dilute it.

A simple way to judge thickness is a **flow test**. Fill a clean plastic cup with a small hole in the base, or an empty syringe with the needle removed, and time how many seconds the product takes to run out. Use the same cup every time. Record the seconds in your batch record. Now "thick" becomes a number you can repeat.

Wash each plate with a clean sponge for the same number of strokes, rinse, and look and feel for oil left behind. You can also count how many greasy plates one measured amount of product washes before the foam disappears. Write the results down. This is how you prove to yourself, and later to buyers, that your product works.

Liquid hand wash, safe bleach use and disinfectant claims

Once your multipurpose liquid soap is consistent, a **liquid hand wash** is a natural second product. It is used many times a day on bare skin, so it must be milder, nicely perfumed and well preserved. This lesson also covers the other thing every cleaning business gets asked about: "Can you make something that kills germs?"
A person washing hands at a sink
Hand wash touches skin many times a day, so mildness and correct pH matter more than foam.
What makes hand wash different
It is usually based mainly on **SLES**, which is gentler on skin than neutralised sulphonic acid.
Many makers add a milder co-surfactant such as **cocamidopropyl betaine** (often called CAPB) to make it softer on hands; ask your supplier for it by name and for its data sheet.
**Glycerine** helps hands feel less dry after washing.
It is thickened mainly with salt (watch the salt curve) and should be close to neutral pH.
Because people dip into it daily, a **preservative** at the supplier's stated dose is essential.
Weigh the SLES and break it into pieces in part of the water; stir gently until fully dissolved. Stirring too hard creates foam that takes hours to settle.
Add the remaining water, the co-surfactant if used, and glycerine; stir gently.
Check pH. Adjust only in very small steps if needed, following your tested formula.
Thicken with salt solution in small portions and use your flow test.
Add perfume, colour and preservative; rest for 12 to 24 hours; check again and bottle in pump bottles.

Before you sell a hand wash, use it yourself several times a day for a week, and ask two or three adults to do the same. Ask them specific questions: does it leave hands tight or dry, is the scent too strong, does the pump dispense easily? Anyone who gets redness or itching should stop using it at once. A milder formula and a lower perfume dose are the usual fixes.
Disinfecting with bleach, safely

For killing germs on hard surfaces at home, household bleach is effective and cheap, so your customers do not need you to invent a disinfectant. Teach them to use it correctly. The US CDC gives this guidance for household bleach containing **5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite**:
Clean the surface with detergent and water first, because dirt protects germs.
Mix 5 tablespoons (one third of a cup) of bleach per gallon of room-temperature water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. That works out to roughly 20 ml of bleach per litre of water.
Leave it on the surface for at least 1 minute before wiping.
Make a fresh solution every day; it loses strength after 24 hours.
Never mix bleach with any other cleaner or disinfectant.
Check the strength on your bottle

Bleach brands sold in Nigeria differ in strength, and some are weaker than 5%. The CDC amounts above are for 5% to 9% bleach. Read the label and follow the manufacturer's dilution directions for disinfecting. If the label gives no strength, follow its directions exactly.

Store bleach in its original opaque bottle with the cap tight, in a cool place away from sunlight, because heat and light make it lose strength. Keep it away from acids, including toilet cleaners and sulphonic acid. Any diluted bleach solution should go in a clearly labelled container, never a drink bottle, and should be thrown away at the end of the day. Bleach also removes colour from clothes and can damage some metals, so warn customers to keep it off fabrics and to rinse metal surfaces after use.

Disinfectant (registered product)

Needs regulatory approval

If your label promises to kill germs, you are selling a disinfectant and must be able to prove it.
Why not make bleach or disinfectants yet?

Some trainers teach making bleach from chlorine chemicals such as calcium hypochlorite, sold as HTH. This involves strong oxidising chemicals and a risk of releasing chlorine gas, and home-made bleach can lose strength quickly in storage, so the customer cannot know how strong it is. Germ-killing products are also checked carefully by regulators. NAFDAC's list of products allowed under its micro-scale scheme includes laundry detergents, soaps and liquid air fresheners, but it does not list disinfectants or bleach. Ask NAFDAC directly before you plan any germ-killing product.

For example, a restaurant owner asks Grace, who sells liquid soap in Ibadan, for "liquid soap that kills 99.9% of germs".
Grace explains that her liquid soap is a cleaner: it removes grease and dirt, which is the first step of hygiene.
She explains that killing germs is a separate step, and recommends a registered bleach diluted according to its label, after washing.
She shows the owner how to make a fresh bleach solution each morning in a labelled container, and to never mix it with the liquid soap or toilet cleaner.
She keeps her own label honest: "multipurpose liquid soap, cuts grease", with no germ claims.
The restaurant gets a safe, correct routine, Grace keeps the order for liquid soap, and she avoids an illegal claim she could not prove.

A product that is good one week and watery the next will lose customers. This module gives you a simple quality testing routine, a fault-fixing guide, the contents of an honest label, the basic NAFDAC registration path for small producers, and the records and waste rules that keep your business safe and trusted.

Set your own written product specification

Big manufacturers test every batch against a **specification**: a short list of measurements the product must meet before it is released. You can do the same with tools that cost very little. Your specification is your promise to customers that the bottle they buy next month will be the same as the one they liked today.

**Sell** only when the batch meets every line of your specification.
**Rework** when the fix is safe and simple, such as adjusting pH or thickness, then test again fully.

Worked example: writing a specification
For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha has made four good test batches of her multipurpose liquid soap and wants a written specification.
She looks at her four records: pH readings were 7, 7, 7 and 8; flow times were 22, 25, 24 and 23 seconds in her syringe test.
She writes: pH 7 to 8; flow time 20 to 26 seconds; clear green, no lumps; passes the grease test; no separation after 7 days.
Her fifth production batch reads pH 7 but flows in 14 seconds, outside her range.
She adds salt solution in small portions, testing after each, until the flow time is 21 seconds, then records the change.
Ifeoma's specification lets her catch a thin batch before it reaches customers, and her record shows exactly what she did to fix it.
Shelf life and expiry dates

Your label needs a best-before or expiry date, and that date should come from evidence, not guesswork. Keep retained samples from your first batches and check them every week for a few months: look for separation, mould, colour change, a sour or musty smell, and changes in thickness and pH. If a sample is still good after three months, you have evidence for a three-month date. Extend the date only as your samples prove it. Products stored in hot shops or in sunlight age faster, so tell resellers to keep them in the shade.
Read pH strips correctly

Use a clean, dry spoon or stick to take a sample, dip the strip briefly, and compare the colour at the time printed on the pack, in daylight. Keep the strip pack tightly closed and dry, because damp strips give wrong readings. Record the number, not just "okay".
Foam is not a quality test
Buyers love foam, but foam alone does not show cleaning power or safety. Use foam only as a feature to describe, and rely on pH, thickness, grease removal and stability to judge quality.

A label does three jobs. It tells the buyer **what the product is and how to use it safely**. It tells the buyer **who made it**, so she can come back or complain. And it shows regulators and big buyers that you are a serious producer. In Nigeria, the **National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)** regulates detergents and other household chemical products, along with food, drugs and cosmetics.

NAFDAC basics for small producers

NAFDAC runs a scheme for **Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)**. Its MSME page lists products allowed under the micro and small scheme, including **laundry detergents, soaps and liquid air fresheners**. The main points it states for micro scale are:
A micro-scale facility has **not more than nine employees**.
**Not more than five products** can be registered under micro scale.

Documents listed include evidence of **CAC registration** (Corporate Affairs Commission), a site use agreement, trademark approval, one vetting sample and three labels, a fumigation certificate and a payment receipt.
The page lists a micro-scale cosmetic fee (41,000 naira at the time of writing). Fees change, so confirm the current amount with NAFDAC before you budget.
The listing certificate is valid for **two years**.

Directions people can follow

Directions should be short, specific and easy to follow. For a multipurpose liquid soap, tell the buyer how much to use for a bowl of washing-up water, how to use it on floors or surfaces, and to rinse well after use. For hand wash, say to apply to wet hands, lather, and rinse. Test your own directions: if one teaspoon in a bowl washes ten oily plates in your grease test, say so. Clear directions also help customers use less product, which makes them trust that your product is concentrated and worth its price.

When NAFDAC inspects a small production site, officers look at whether the place is clean and organised, whether raw materials and finished goods are stored properly, whether workers use protective equipment, and whether you keep records. The habits in this course, a safety station, labelled containers, batch records and retained samples, are exactly the kind of good practice that makes an inspection easier.

Batch records, safe storage and responsible waste
Keep a batch record that lets you trace any bottle back to its raw materials
Store raw materials and finished products safely
Dispose of chemical waste and rinse water responsibly
Make fair, safe choices that protect customers and neighbours

Records are what turn a kitchen experiment into a business. When a customer says "the last keg was too thin", a batch record tells you exactly what went into that keg, who supplied it, and what the tests showed. Good records also show NAFDAC inspectors and large buyers that you work carefully.
A person working on a spreadsheet
A simple batch record in a notebook or spreadsheet lets you trace every bottle back to its ingredients.
What goes in a batch record
Batch number, for example LS-2611-03 (product, year and month, batch of the month).
Date, batch size, and who made it.
Each raw material: name, supplier, strength, and the amount actually used.
Any extra alkali or salt added during adjustments, and why.
Test results: pH, flow time, appearance, grease test, and stability check after a week.
Number of bottles or kegs filled, and the decision: released, reworked or discarded.
Any safety incident or near miss, and the fix.
Worked example: tracing a complaint
For example, a school bursar in Abuja tells Amaka that the last two kegs of her liquid soap stung the cleaners' hands.
Amaka reads the batch number on the kegs: LS-2610-04.
Her record shows that batch used a new drum of sulphonic acid and was bottled with pH 6, which is below her specification of 7 to 8. She had been in a hurry and skipped the final check.
She tests the retained sample: pH 6. The cause is clear.
She replaces the two kegs free, corrects the remaining stock to pH 7, and adds "final pH check signed before bottling" to her routine.
Because of her records, Amaka found the cause in minutes, kept the school's trust, and changed her process so it does not happen again.
Storage
Keep acids (sulphonic acid) and alkalis (caustic soda, soda ash) on separate shelves, with lids tight.
Store everything off the floor, out of direct sun, and locked away from children.
Keep finished products separate from raw materials, and food completely separate from both.
Use first-in, first-out: sell older batches before newer ones.
Waste and the environment

Detergent ingredients can harm streams, fish and wells when they arrive in concentrated form. Phosphate builders such as STPP can feed algae in rivers and lakes, which is one reason many countries have limited phosphates in detergents. Your waste will be small, but handle it with care.
Never pour concentrated sulphonic acid or caustic soda into drains, gutters, soil or near a well or borehole.
Leftover small amounts of acid or alkali can be slowly added to a large volume of your batch water during the next production, where they will be neutralised, or kept labelled until you can use them.
Rinse water from washing equipment is dilute; pour it into a proper drain or soakaway, away from wells.
Rinse empty chemical containers, puncture or mark them, and never give them away for storing water, oil or food.
Use only as much STPP as your tested formula needs; consider whether soda ash alone is enough where water is soft.

Plan: high harm, harder
Quick win: low harm, easy
Later: low harm, harder
Effort to fix
Possible harm
Rank your risks by harm and effort, and fix the high-harm, easy items immediately.
Fair and safe choices
Do not water down product to make more money while selling it as the same product. If you sell a cheaper, thinner grade, label and price it as such.
Do not use formalin or unknown chemicals because they are cheap.
Do not employ children to handle chemicals. Train any helper in PPE and first aid, and record that training.
Respect neighbours: mix where fumes will not blow into homes, and do not leave containers where children play.

As orders grow you may bring in a helper. Before she touches any chemical, show her the safety card, the PPE, the mixing order, the bleach rule and first aid. Let her watch one full batch, then make one under your supervision. Write the date and what you trained in your notebook and ask her to sign it. Keep an **incident log** in the same notebook: every splash, spill or near miss, what caused it and what you changed. A near miss written down today prevents an injury tomorrow.

Every jug, bucket and drum that holds a chemical or solution, even for an hour, should carry a label with what it is. Unlabelled caustic solution looks exactly like water. Use masking tape and a marker, and remove the label only after the container is washed.

Costing a batch and pricing for profit

Many liquid soap sellers know the price of sulphonic acid but have never added up the cost of bottles, labels, transport and their own time. They feel busy but cannot find the profit. In this lesson you will cost a batch completely, then price from that number, not from what the next seller charges.
A bag of money
Profit is what is left after every cost, including packaging and transport, has been counted.
The four groups of cost
**Raw materials:** every chemical in the batch at the price you actually paid, including colour, perfume and preservative.
**Packaging:** bottles or kegs, caps, labels or stickers, and cartons or nylon for delivery.
**Overheads per batch:** transport to the market, PPE replacement, pH strips, water, a share of equipment wear, and phone data for marketing.
**Your labour:** a fair amount for your hours. If you do not count it, you cannot later afford to pay a helper.
Worked example: costing a 25-litre batch
For example, Grace in Ibadan makes 25 litres of multipurpose liquid soap. All prices are illustrative and approximate; use your own receipts.
Raw materials for the batch (all chemicals, perfume, colour, preservative): 21,000 naira (approximate).
Packaging: 25 one-litre bottles with caps at 250 naira each = 6,250 naira; 25 labels at 60 naira = 1,500 naira. Total 7,750 naira.
Overheads for the batch (transport, pH strips, PPE wear, data): 3,000 naira.
Labour: 4 hours at 1,000 naira per hour = 4,000 naira.
Full batch cost: 21,000 + 7,750 + 3,000 + 4,000 = 35,750 naira. Cost per 1-litre bottle: 35,750 / 25 = 1,430 naira.
Grace knows each bottle costs her about 1,430 naira. Any price below that loses money, even if she is selling a lot.
From cost to price

Decide the **margin** you need: the share of the selling price that is profit. A simple method is **cost divided by (1 minus margin)**. For a 30% margin on a cost of 1,430 naira: 1,430 / 0.70 = about 2,043 naira, so Grace might price at 2,000 to 2,100 naira. Then compare with prices in your area. If similar quality sells for much less, look for savings in packaging or buying, not in the surfactant that does the cleaning.

When raw material prices rise

Chemical prices in Nigeria can change quickly, often with the exchange rate, because many raw materials are imported. Recalculate your batch cost every time you buy a new stock of raw materials. If cost rises, you have three honest choices: raise the price, change the pack size and tell customers, or accept a smaller margin for a short time. Diluting the product while keeping the same label is not an honest choice.
Break-even: how many bottles before you profit?

Your first equipment, such as drums, a scale, PPE and a stock of bottles, is a one-time **start-up cost**. To know when it is paid back, divide it by the profit you make on each bottle. For example, if Grace spent 45,000 naira (approximate) on equipment and makes about 600 naira profit on each 1-litre bottle, she needs to sell 45,000 / 600 = 75 bottles to recover her start-up money. After that, the profit is truly hers. Knowing this number helps you set a realistic sales target for your first two or three months.

Buying raw materials in larger packs is often cheaper per kilogram, but it ties up cash, and some materials, such as preservatives and perfume, have a limited shelf life. Buy bigger packs only for items you use every batch and can store safely, and only when you have regular orders to justify it.
Keep a one-page cost sheet
List every item with the price paid and the date. Update it with each purchase. A cost sheet on your phone lets you answer a bulk buyer's price request on the spot without guessing.

Finally, count only **good** containers. If two bottles leak or a batch is reworked, the cost of that loss is shared by the bottles you can actually sell. Track your losses for a few batches and include an average waste figure in your costing.

How cleaning works
The surfactant: two different ends
Head loves water
Tail loves oil and grease
Tails wrap each drop of oil
Water rinses the grease away
Every cleaning product depends on one kind of ingredient, a surfactant. That word is short for surface active agent. One end, the head, loves water.
The other end, the tail, loves oil and grease, and hates water.
When you wash a greasy pot, the tails push into the grease, and thousands of molecules surround each small drop of oil.
Now the grease has a coat that water can hold, so rinsing carries it away. That is why plain water cannot remove palm oil from a plate, but water with detergent can.

Sulphonic acid is a thick, dark brown, oily liquid. As bought, it is a strong, corrosive acid. It only becomes a cleaning agent after it is neutralised with an alkali.
SLES, often sold as texapon, is gentler on skin and foams well. A label saying 70% means 100 g of paste holds about 70 g of real surfactant. Buy on known strength, not just price.
Caustic soda is a strong alkali used to neutralise the acid. Soda ash is milder, and fizzes when it meets acid.
STPP is a builder. It ties up the minerals in hard water so the surfactant works better.
Nitrosol, CMC and salt give the product body. Remember, more foam does not mean better cleaning.
Many local recipes use formalin as a preservative. Formaldehyde is classed as a human carcinogen, so avoid it. Use a detergent preservative at the dose on its data sheet.

Add the caustic soda slowly to the water, stirring. Never pour water onto caustic soda. It can boil up and splash.
The solution gets very hot. Let it cool before adding it to anything.
Pour sulphonic acid slowly into the water or batch, never the other way round.

Mixed with ammonia, found in some glass cleaners and urine, it releases chloramine gases. Both can damage the lungs and kill.

Your specification
pH with a test strip
Thickness: flow test in seconds
Cleaning: grease test on oily plates
Stability: sealed sample for a week

A product that is good one week and watery the next will lose customers. So test every batch against a specification, a short list of measurements it must meet. First, pH, read at the time printed on the strip pack.
Second, thickness, with the same flow test every time.
Third, look at a sample in a clear bottle against light, and smell it.
Fourth, the grease test on oily plates. Foam is not a quality test.
Fifth, stability. Keep a sealed, labelled sample from every batch, and watch it for at least a week. If a customer complains, you can check that same batch.
Worked example
Ifeoma writes her specification
Fix one thing at a time, then retest and record
Four good batches: pH 7 to 8
Flow time 20 to 26 seconds
Batch five flows in 14 seconds
Adds salt solution in small portions
Now 21 seconds: in range, recorded
For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha looks at four good test batches. Her pH readings were 7, 7, 7 and 8. So she writes pH 7 to 8.
Her flow times were between 22 and 25 seconds, so she writes 20 to 26 seconds. She adds clear green, no lumps, passes the grease test, and no separation after 7 days.
Her fifth batch reads pH 7, but flows in 14 seconds. Too thin. Outside her range.
She adds salt solution in small portions, testing after each.
At 21 seconds it is back in range, and she records the change. She caught a thin batch before it reached a customer.
Decide
Only when the batch meets every line of your specification.
When the fix is safe and simple, like pH or thickness. Then test again fully.
Mould, bad smell, unknown contamination, or a cause you cannot find.
Sell a batch only when it meets every line of your specification.
Rework it when the fix is safe and simple, such as adjusting pH or thickness. Then run every test again. A batch that stings hands is never sold.
Discard it when there is mould, a bad smell, or a problem you cannot explain. Never sell a doubtful batch cheaply. A bad product still carries your name.
Honest claims
What you can and cannot say
Fine, if true
Near neutral pH, if tested
Antibacterial or antiseptic
100% natural or chemical free
Safe for babies, without proof
Your label tells the buyer what the product is, how to use it safely, and who made it. Only claim what you can prove. Cuts grease, works in hard water, or near neutral pH if you tested it.
Do not say kills 99.9% of germs, or antibacterial. That is a disinfectant claim. And do not say chemical free. Everything is made of chemicals.
Your label
What goes on the label
Product name, brand, phone number
Net contents and main ingredients
Directions for use
Warnings: children, eyes, no bleach
Batch number, dates
NAFDAC number, only once given
Put the product name, your brand and phone number, the net contents and main ingredients, and clear directions.
Add warnings. Keep out of reach of children. Rinse eyes with plenty of water. If swallowed, do not induce vomiting. Do not mix with bleach. Do not transfer into drink bottles.
Add the batch number, production date and a best-before date your samples prove. And never print a NAFDAC number you have not been given.
NAFDAC basics
The micro-scale path
Pay only through official NAFDAC channels
Register your business name with CAC

NAFDAC regulates detergents in Nigeria. Its micro-scale scheme lists laundry detergents and soaps. Micro scale means not more than nine employees and not more than five products. First, get a stable formula and good records.
Register your business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission, CAC.
Keep a clean site, with labels ready.
Then apply. Fees change, so confirm the current amount with NAFDAC before you budget.
Officers inspect your site and review a sample. Be careful of anyone offering to get you a number in a few days. A fake number can lead to seizure of goods and prosecution.
Records and waste
Responsible production
Number and record every batch
Acids and alkalis on separate shelves
No concentrated chemicals in drains
Never reuse chemical containers for food
Never water down product secretly

Give every batch a number and a record. For example, when a school bursar in Abuja says two kegs stung the cleaners' hands, Amaka reads batch LS-2610-04. It was bottled at pH 6. She replaces the kegs free and adds a signed final pH check.

Store acids and alkalis apart, locked and off the floor. Never pour concentrated chemicals into drains or near wells. Never give away chemical containers for water or food. And never water down your product secretly.

Why this matters
Busy, but where is the profit?
Raw materials, at the price you paid
Packaging: bottles, caps, labels

Your labour, so you can pay a helper later

Many sellers know the price of sulphonic acid, but never add up bottles, labels, transport and their own time. They feel busy, but cannot find the profit. Cost has four groups. First, raw materials, at the price you actually paid.
Second, packaging: bottles or kegs, caps, labels and cartons.
Third, overheads: transport, pH strips, PPE wear and phone data.
Fourth, your labour. If you do not count it, you can never afford to pay a helper.
Worked example
Costing a 25-litre batch
For example, Grace in Ibadan makes 25 litres of multipurpose liquid soap in 1-litre bottles.
Packaging: bottles and labels
Labour: 4 hours
Naira prices are approximate.
For example, Grace in Ibadan makes 25 litres of liquid soap. These prices are approximate, so use your own receipts.
All the chemicals, perfume, colour and preservative cost 21,000 naira.
Bottles with caps at 250 naira each, and labels at 60 naira, come to 7,750 naira.
Overheads for the batch are 3,000 naira.
Her labour is 4 hours at 1,000 naira an hour, so 4,000 naira.
The full batch costs 35,750 naira. Divided by 25 bottles, each bottle costs her about 1,430 naira. Any price below that loses money, however much she sells.
Price with a clear margin
Never dilute the product and keep the same label
Cost per bottle: 1,430 naira
Margin 30%: divide by 0.70
About 2,043 naira; price 2,000 to 2,100
Compare with prices in your area
Recalculate with every new stock
Now price from cost, not from what the next seller charges. Grace's bottle costs 1,430 naira.
She wants a 30% margin, so she divides the cost by 0.70.
That is about 2,043 naira, so she might price at 2,000 to 2,100.
Then compare with local prices. If similar quality sells for much less, save on packaging or buying, not on the surfactant that does the cleaning.

Chemical prices change quickly, so recalculate with every new stock. If cost rises, raise the price, change the pack size and tell customers, or accept a smaller margin for a while. Secretly diluting is not an honest choice.
Break-even
When is your start-up paid back?
Start-up cost: 45,000 naira
Profit per bottle: about 600 naira
45,000 divided by 600 = 75 bottles
After that, the profit is truly yours
Drums, a scale, PPE and a first stock of bottles are a one-time start-up cost. For example, Grace spent 45,000 naira.
She makes about 600 naira profit on each bottle.
So 45,000 divided by 600 is 75 bottles to recover her start-up money.
After that, the profit is truly hers. This number gives her a realistic sales target.
Selling
The side-by-side grease demo
Specific, tested benefits. No germ or medical claims.
Two greasy plates, two bowls, a spoon
One spoon of your product per bowl
Same strokes; the buyer feels both plates
Show your label and batch number
Offer a trial size; agree a delivery day
Your real goal is repeat customers. The strongest sales tool is a demo. Bring two plates with palm oil grease, two bowls and a measuring spoon.
Measure one spoon of your product into a bowl of water. Ask the buyer to use her current product in the other bowl.
Wash one plate in each bowl with the same number of strokes, and let her feel both plates.
Show your label: ingredients, warnings, batch number and phone number.
Offer a trial size and agree a delivery day. For example, Amaka in Abuja does a demo on a restaurant's own soup pot and leaves a 4-litre container. Now she delivers about 50 litres a month.
Safe selling
Protect yourself and your buyers
Confirm money in your own account
Carry kegs upright, caps tight
Refills only in labelled containers
Never fill drink bottles
Keep customer numbers private
Confirm the money has actually arrived in your account before you release goods. Fake transfer screenshots are a common scam.
Carry kegs upright with caps tight. Refill only into a clean, correctly labelled container, and never into drink bottles. And keep customers' numbers and addresses private.
